To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hydrothermal circulation driven by groundwater discharge can account for the formation of valley networks and the crustal magnetism of Mars.

1) Hydrothermal systems on Mars can be sustained by groundwater discharge from valley networks and by intrusion-driven groundwater flow; 2) Intrusion-driven groundwater flow is capable of generating hydrothermal systems that can explain the observed valley network discharge; and 3) The hydrologic and hydrothermal systems on Mars are capable of sustaining the observed magnetic anomalies on Mars.

hydrothermal discharge can be an important component of the Martian hydrologic cycle, with implications for the formation of the Martian crust and valley networks, and that hydrothermal discharge is capable of generating magnetic anomalies of the type observed in the southern highlands.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of hydrothermal systems in the evolution of Mars.
the formation of the Martian crustal magnetic field, and the role of hydrothermal systems in the formation of the valley networks, the formation of the crustal magnetism.
understanding the controls on hydrothermal activity on Mars, and the role hydrothermal systems played in the formation of valley networks and magnetic anomalies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Martian hydrothermal systems are capable of generating the runoff necessary to produce the valley network system and are also capable of generating the intrusions necessary to produce the magnetic anomalies.
the Martian crust is not a single, homogeneous layer.
the formation of Martian valley networks and the associated valley network runoff discharge is not a prerequisite for the formation of the magnetic anomalies in the Martian crust.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Martian hydrological cycle is not as simple as it is often portrayed in textbooks.
the hydrologic and geologic processes that formed the valleys of Mars were also likely responsible for the crustal magnetism.
we show that groundwater flow on early Mars was a significant agent of erosion, and that groundwater flow was also a likely source for the magnetic anomalies on the Martian surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the formation of the Martian magnetic anomalies is consistent with the formation of the valleys, and that these processes may have occurred at similar times and rates.
hydrothermal discharge is a plausible mechanism for the formation of valley networks and magnetic anomalies.
the formation of valley networks on Mars was likely controlled by hydrothermal systems, and not just by the presence of water.
